title: Mental health and faith
hookLine: Muslim voices encouraging therapy alongside prayer

lines: DOES IT MEAN MY FAITH IS WEAK?
A FATHER AND A LOST SON.
cards: If I need a therapist, does that mean my faith is weak? Some imams hear that after the prayer, quietly, by the shoe racks, and some now answer: pray, yes, and also see someone.
Some Muslim counselors and therapists work with both in the room, the prayer mat and the treatment plan. The question underneath is old: can a person of deep faith be crushed by sorrow?
The Qur'an answers with a father, and a son he thought he'd lost.

teach.b: In Surah Yusuf, the prophet Ya'qub loses his beloved son Yusuf, and later another son too. He turns away from the others, the surah says, and his eyes go white with sorrow. His sons tell him he'll grieve himself to death.
He answers, in paraphrase, that he lays out his distress and his grief to Allah alone. He is a prophet, and he is not okay. The Qur'an doesn't hide his grief or call it a failure.
And he names it, out loud, to God. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wept too.

teach.h: THE EYES SHED TEARS, THE HEART GRIEVES.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, when his infant son Ibrahim was dying, his eyes filled with tears; when a companion was surprised, he said, in paraphrase: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
Then a short report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi.
A man asks whether he should tie up his camel and trust in God, or leave it loose and trust. The answer: tie it, and trust. Trust is not instead of action.
Prayer is not instead of care. So when someone with depression keeps both their prayers and their therapy appointment, some Muslim counselors would say they're tying the camel.
The Arabic word for heart is qalb, and the Qur'an speaks of hearts that are sick and hearts that find rest. In that reading, healing it two ways isn't doubting God.

And said plainly: if the heaviness is taking your sleep or your hope, or you've thought about not being here, please reach for help today. In the US, call or text 988; elsewhere, local emergency help.

how: Some imams now refer people to counselors, and Muslim therapists and support lines offer care that makes room for prayer and faith alongside treatment.

games.q: what does “mental health and faith” mean?
o: a sign that someone's faith has grown weak or thin
caring for the heart with both prayer and real treatment
the belief that enough prayer replaces any therapy

games.q: healing two ways — tap the pairs.
p: the eyes shed tears, the heart grieves

s: in the Qur'an, Ya'qub hides his grief because a prophet shouldn't feel it
his eyes go white with sorrow, and he names his distress to God out loud.
the Prophet wept when his son Ibrahim was dying
the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, he said, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
tie your camel and trust means trust is enough on its own
the answer is tie it, and trust: action and trust together.

games.q: you've ridden your camel to the mosque. do you tie it up and trust in God, or leave it loose and trust in God?
o: leave it loose: trust is enough.
games.why: the answer in Jami' at-Tirmidhi is tie it, and trust. today that report is sometimes used to explain why prayer and therapy can go together.

practice: Ask yourself honestly how your heart is today, in a real word: tired, heavy, restless, light. Then bring to mind one person who's gone quiet lately, and one sentence you could send them: how are you, really?
If you pray, name your distress, and theirs, to God, the way Ya'qub did; if you don't, just name it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Mental health and faith. Grief and distress held by prophets in the Qur'an and hadith, and healed two ways: prayer and care. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the heart, the word the Qur'an uses for hearts that are sick and hearts that find rest.

carryVoice: Your line: heal the heart two ways. Prayer and care, together. Be gentle with yourself.

sources.ref: Qur'an 12:86 (Ya'qub lays out his distress and grief to Allah alone)
Qur'an 12:84–85 (Ya'qub's eyes whitened with sorrow; his sons fear he will grieve to death)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 (the Prophet's tears at the death of his son Ibrahim)
